content: The evidence presented evaluates the use of chest X-ray (CXR) and molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) for tuberculosis (TB) screening among people living with HIV (PLHIV). Below is a detailed explanation of the findings and recommendations: 1. Chest X-ray (CXR) Evidence and Cost-Effectiveness: Six studies were reviewed, five of which were of high quality, while one was of lower quality. The evidence was indirect, and there was consistency in unit costs for CXR, but variability in screening algorithms and outcomes. The cost per patient diagnosed with TB ranged from $40 to $549, depending on the study and setting. For example, in South Africa and Russia, the use of CXR following the WHO-recommended 4-symptom screen (W4SS) was shown to be cost-effective. In South Africa, combining W4SS with smear microscopy, CXR, and Xpert testing was cost-effective, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of $360 per additional TB case diagnosed. Similarly, in Russia, mass CXR screening using mobile units was cost-effective, with an ICER of $549 per additional TB case diagnosed. In sub-Saharan Africa, the use of CXR following W4SS and smear microscopy was cost-effective, with an ICER of $7,775 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). In Uganda, using CXR as a triage test followed by Xpert diagnosis was cost-effective, with an ICER of $610 per year of life saved. 2. Equity Considerations: Access to CXR is limited in many lowand middle-income countries, particularly in rural areas, due to the lack of decentralization. This results in high costs and time burdens for patients traveling to district or national centers for screening. Compared to W4SS, CXR results are less influenced by response bias, discrimination, or stigma. While increased sensitivity of CXR may lead to higher costs due to unnecessary follow-up investigations, it also identifies more TB cases, reducing disease burden, mortality, and impoverishment. Scaling up access to CXR, including mobile X-ray units, is necessary to improve equity. However, in the absence of mobile X-rays, equity may be reduced due to variability in access and potential out-of-pocket expenses for transport and testing. 3. Acceptability and Feasibility: There is limited qualitative evidence on the acceptability of CXR among PLHIV. However, stigma related to HIV and TB may complicate decision-making for individuals. CXR is not yet decentralized in many high TB burden settings due to infrastructure and human resource limitations. However, systematic screening using mobile digital X-ray services integrated into national programs has been shown to be feasible and scalable in some settings. Ownership of X-ray machines can affect access, particularly in terms of costs to end-users. 4. WHO Recommendations for CXR: WHO recommends the use of CXR in parallel with W4SS to assist in ruling out active TB before initiating TB preventive treatment (TPT) among PLHIV on antiretroviral therapy (ART), where CXR is available. CXR alone has similar or higher sensitivity and specificity compared to W4SS across all sub-populations. When combined with W4SS, the sensitivity is higher or similar, with comparable specificity. For pregnant women, CXR poses no significant risk to the fetus if good practices are observed, as the primary beam is directed away from the pelvis. 5. Implementation Considerations: Countries should position CXR within national TB screening algorithms based on feasibility, available resources, health system capacity, and equity. A baseline CXR could be included as part of initial enrollment in ART services. However, W4SS should always be conducted as part of a comprehensive clinical evaluation, regardless of CXR availability. Lack of access to CXR should not be a barrier to initiating TPT. Screening should align with HIV services, such as annual check-ups and viral load monitoring. 6. Molecular WHO-Recommended Rapid Diagnostic Tests (mWRDs): mWRDs were assessed for accuracy compared to W4SS followed by mWRD. For inpatients with HIV, W4SS alone had a sensitivity of 96% but a specificity of only 11%, limiting its utility in this population. In hypothetical populations of 1,000 PLHIV with varying TB prevalence (10%, 20%, and 30%), mWRDs correctly classified more true positives and fewer false negatives compared to W4SS followed by mWRD. However, the added utility of mWRDs was limited due to the low specificity of W4SS in these populations. 7. Desirable and Undesirable Effects: Desirable effects include timely identification and treatment of active TB cases, reducing transmission and mortality, and identifying individuals eligible for TPT or ART. Undesirable effects include false positives, leading to inappropriate treatment and delays in ART initiation, and false negatives, resulting in missed treatment opportunities, continued transmission, and increased mortality risk. 8. Research Gaps: Further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness and accuracy of combining W4SS, CXR, mWRDs, and other diagnostic tools in different sequences. Additionally, the optimal frequency of routine CXR screening among PLHIV in care should be determined. In conclusion, CXR is recommended as a screening tool for TB among adults and adolescents living with HIV, particularly when used in combination with W4SS. However, its implementation should consider feasibility, equity, and resource availability. Molecular diagnostic tests offer additional utility but may have limited added value in certain populations.
